div.head: II Atr Prol.
div.ab: Ðis synd ða friðmal ⁊ ða forword, ðe Æthelred cyng ⁊ ealle his witan wið ðone here gedon habbað, ðe Anlaf ⁊ Iustin ⁊ Guðmund Stegitan sunu mid wæron.
Hęc sunt uerba pacis et prolocutiones, quas Æþelredus rex et omnes sapientes eius cum exercitu firmauerunt, qui cum Analauo et Iustino et Guðmundo Stegitam filio uenit.
Ðis synd ða friðmal ⁊ ða forword ðe Æthelred cyng ⁊ ealle his witan wið ðone here gedon habbað, ðe Anlaf ⁊ Iustin ⁊ Guðmund Stegitan sunu mid wæron.

II Atr. Prolog. Dies sind die Friedensschlüsse und die Verträge, die König Aethelred und alle seine Witan mit dem Heere [der Nordleute] gemacht haben, bei welchem Olaf [Tryggvason aus Norwegen] und Josteinn und Guðmund Stegitas[?] Sohn waren.

II Atr. Prologue. These are the peace-terms and the agreements which King Æthelred and all his witan have made with the army [of the Northmen] with which Olaf [Tryggvason of Norway] and Jósteinn and Guthmund son of Stegita[?] were.
These are the terms of the truce and the agreement which King Æthelred and all his councillors have made with the (Viking) fleet led by Olaf and Justin and Guðmund, the son of Stegita.
These are the peace terms and conditions which King Ethelred and all his councillors have made with the army with which were Olaf and Jostein and Guthmund, Steita’s son.

Das Heer selbst war wesentlich Dänisch. Es zeigt, im Ggs. zum Englischen Vertragschliesser, keinen vornehmen Rat neben seinen Führern; ebenso o. zu AGu Einl. 4. Regelmässig befehligen es mehrere Führer; Steenstrup Études prélim. à l’hist. Norm. 196. Auf Englischer Seite treten Witan auf. Über die Identität s. Maurer Höldur 200; Bekehrung Norweg. I 277

The army itself was essentially Danish. In contrast to the English party to the treaty, it shows no council of nobles alongside its leaders; likewise above on AGu Introduction 4. It is regularly commanded by several leaders; Steenstrup Études prélim. à l’hist. Norm. 196. On the English side Witan appear. On the identity see Maurer Höldur 200; Bekehrung Norweg. I 277

Da B, Florenz und wahrscheinlich Q i -an als Gen. nehmen, kann der Name nur in a enden. Er ist sonst nicht bezeugt. Bugge Norges hist. I 2 p. 245 vermutet ‘Stigand’: unrichtig, denn dieser Name war Engländern geläufig, ward also nicht verderbt.—Vielleicht hatte das Original Scegia d. i. Skeggi's (s. d. Gl); der Name steht u. a. Njal saga ed. Vigfusson Icel. sagas I 339. Dagegen denkt Björkman (Nord. Personenna. in Engl. 131) an gen. Stegnan, von westnord. Steini, wobei it statt n verschrieben wäre

Since B, Florence and probably Q i take -an as gen., the name can only end in a. It is not otherwise attested. Bugge Norges hist. I 2 p. 245 conjectures ‘Stigand’: wrongly, for this name was familiar to the English and so would not have been corrupted.—Perhaps the original had Scegia, i.e. Skeggi’s (see that word in Gl); the name occurs, among other places, in Njal saga ed. Vigfusson Icel. sagas I 339. Björkman (Nord. Personenna. in Engl. 131), on the other hand, thinks of gen. Stegnan, from West Norse Steini, in which case it would have been miswritten for n

‘Söhne’ Freeman Norm. conq. I 270; allein es scheint beispiellos, dass von zwei Brüdern nur dem zweiten der Vatersname beigegeben wird; ja dann könnte man auch Olaf als Bruder verstehen: was er sicher nicht war

‘Sons’ Freeman Norm. conq. I 270; but it seems unparalleled for only the second of two brothers to be given the father’s name; indeed, Olaf could then also be understood as a brother: which he certainly was not

The well-known Olaf Tryggvason, afterwards King of Norway, 995–1000. Before his acquisition of the throne he spent some years in piracy in the west, cf. Sax. Chr. 993 A, 994 E. Detailed accounts of his life, based on tradition, are to be found in Norse literature, especially in Snorri’s Saga of Olaf Tryggvason (Heimskringla) and in the longer saga of Olaf Tryggvason preserved in the Flateyjarbók and elsewhere, both of which (the second in an abridged form) have been translated into English. He is also very frequently mentioned in the Islendiga Sögur.
Justin, Norse Josteinn, was the brother of Ástríðr, the mother of Olaf Tryggvason (see Olafssaga Tr. in the Heimskringla, Chaps. 58, 102).
Guthmund, the son of Stegita, is mentioned by Florence of Worcester, but beyond this nothing definite seems to be known about him.

This treaty may be compared with Alfred’s treaty with Guthrum (No. 34), for the two English kings face some similar problems. But the later treaty is concerned also with the safety of English ships in foreign ports, and thus affords evidence for English trade. If the terms mentioned in chap, 1 as made by Archbishop Sigeric, Ealdorman Æthelweard and Ealdorman Ælfric are those of this treaty, this was drawn up no later than the death of Sigeric about 28 October 994 (see p. 236, n. 3), and this was before the end of the invasion of 994, and one would have to date the treaty as soon after the events of 991 described in the Chronicle. But E.V. Gordon may have been right in arguing that the terms in chap, 1 are those of previous, local treaties, which are now incorporated into a general treaty, after the invasion of 994 was over. The treaty survives only in the twelfthcentury manuscript, C.C.C.C. 383, and in Quadripartitus. Rubrics supplied by Lambard have no authority, and I omit them. It is edited by Liebermann, I, 220–5; and with English translation by Robertson, pp. 56–61, Thorpe, I, 284–9. [Her footnote 5: Mod. Lang. Rev., xxxii (1937), 24–32]
